annotations.text:
LLM-based world models enable scalable training and evaluation of web agents through simulated trajectories, but suffer from rollout drift where simulated behavior diverges from real environments. We investigate the root cause of this drift in text-based world models and discover that 100% of first divergences occur at search-result observations, with search results exhibiting a 99.8% per-step divergence rate. Based on this finding, we propose search-anchored hybrid rollouts, a minimal intervention that grounds search observations with real data while keeping other observations simulated. On WebShop, our method improves Consistency Ratio from 0.594 to 0.824, a +38.7% relative improvement. Notably, anchoring only the first search provides negligible benefit, while anchoring all searches yields substantial gains, confirming that compounding search errors drive rollout drift. Our approach outperforms agent-side baselines and demonstrates that targeted observation grounding can effectively address world model limitations without requiring model improvements.
WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system. The code is publicly available.<sup>1</sup>
annotations.comment:
Paragraph role: Abstract providing compact problem -> gap -> method -> result summary.

Diagnosis: The abstract is mostly self-contained and well-structured, but the `WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system. The code is publicly available.` (line 5) is out of place in the abstract flow and will reduce academic credibility. Additionally, CR improvement is stated as +38.7% relative improvement (0.594 to 0.824), which is arithmetic-consistent ((0.824-0.594)/0.594 ≈ 0.387), but the abstract does not state what world model/agent backbone was used. Without this, readers cannot calibrate the difficulty of the task or the cost of the improvement.

Impact: The WARNING notice disrupts the narrative and may cause readers to discount results prematurely. Missing backbone specification reduces reproducibility framing.

Actionable fix: (a) Move the WARNING to a footnote or end-of-paper acknowledgement rather than inline in the abstract. (b) Add one clause specifying the world model backbone and agent used (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B world model + Gemini-2.5-Flash agent).

Mentor Revised Version:
LLM-based world models enable scalable training and evaluation of web agents through simulated trajectories, but suffer from rollout drift where simulated behavior diverges from real environments. We identify the root cause of this drift in text-based world models: 100% of first divergences occur at search-result observations, with a 99.8% per-step divergence rate. Based on this finding, we propose search-anchored hybrid rollouts, which ground search observations with real BM25-retrieved data while keeping other observations simulated. Using a Qwen2.5-7B world model and Gemini-2.5-Flash agent on WebShop, our method improves Consistency Ratio from 0.594 to 0.824 (+38.7%), with benefits scaling for multi-search episodes. Anchoring only the first search provides negligible benefit, confirming that compounding search errors drive rollout drift.
annotations.summary: Abstract needs backbone specification and WARNING relocation for credibility and reproducibility.

annotations.text: World models offer a promising path toward scalable training and evaluation of web agents by simulating environment dynamics without costly real-world interactions (Li et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Chae et al., 2024). By generating synthetic trajectories, world models can enable action verification, policy learning, and safe exploration in complex web environments (Deng et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023). However, LLM-based world models suffer from rollout drift: simulated trajectories progressively diverge from real environment behavior, limiting their utility for downstream applications.
annotations.comment:
Paragraph role: Big picture and problem statement establishing world models for web agents and the rollout drift problem.

Diagnosis: This paragraph correctly sets the context and defines the problem (rollout drift). The citations (Li et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Chae et al., 2024) are well-matched. However, the definition of "rollout drift" is descriptive but not precise enough. The reader cannot distinguish rollout drift from general simulation-error accumulation without a clear definition. The paragraph does not state what makes this problem research-worthy beyond "limiting their utility."

Impact: Without a crisp definition and stakes framing, the reader may not grasp why this is a pressing problem that needs a specialized solution rather than a general world model improvement.

Actionable fix: Add one sentence defining rollout drift (e.g., "simulated trajectories that diverge from real environment observations after only a few steps") and one sentence on why it matters practically (e.g., "making synthetic trajectory generation unreliable for planning, verification, or data synthesis").

Mentor Revised Version:
World models offer a promising path toward scalable training and evaluation of web agents by simulating environment dynamics without costly real-world interactions (Li et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Chae et al., 2024). By generating synthetic trajectories, world models can enable action verification, policy learning, and safe exploration in complex web environments (Deng et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023). However, LLM-based world models suffer from rollout drift: simulated trajectories progressively diverge from real environment observations after only a few steps, making synthetic trajectories unreliable for planning, verification, or data synthesis.
annotations.summary: Intro P1 needs sharper rollout-drift definition and clearer practical stakes for reader engagement.

annotations.text: We investigate the root cause of rollout drift in text-based world models for web agents. Through systematic error analysis on WebShop (Yao et al., 2022a), we discover that 100% of first divergences occur at search-result observations, with search results exhibiting a 99.8% per-step divergence rate. This finding reveals that search-result simulation—not general state prediction—is the primary failure mode. The world model generates hallucinated product ASINs and descriptions that differ from the real search engine results, causing cascading errors as the agent interacts with non-existent products.
annotations.comment:
Paragraph role: Core diagnostic finding — identifying search-result simulation as the primary failure mode.

Diagnosis: The claim "100% of first divergences occur at search-result observations, with search results exhibiting a 99.8% per-step divergence rate" is very strong. This is the central empirical finding that justifies the entire method. However, the paragraph does not clarify how divergence is measured (exact match? semantic similarity?) or how the per-step rate is computed (over what denominator?). Without this operational definition, the 99.8% statistic cannot be independently verified by the reader.

Impact: An unverifiable 99.8% divergence rate undermines confidence in the subsequent methodological design. Reviewers may question whether the metric is overly strict (e.g., token-level exact match) or whether the evaluation protocol is fair.

Actionable fix: Add one sentence specifying the divergence measurement protocol. For example: "We measure divergence as token-level mismatch between world model predictions and real environment observations at each step. The 99.8% rate is computed over all search-result steps across 200 test episodes."

Mentor Revised Version:
We investigate the root cause of rollout drift in text-based world models for web agents. Through systematic error analysis on WebShop (Yao et al., 2022a), we measure divergence as token-level mismatch between world model predictions and real environment observations. We find that 100% of first divergences occur at search-result observations, with search results exhibiting a 99.8% per-step divergence rate over 200 test episodes. This reveals that search-result simulation—not general state prediction—is the primary failure mode: the world model generates hallucinated product ASINs and descriptions that differ from real search engine results, causing cascading errors as the agent interacts with non-existent products.
annotations.summary: Intro P2's 99.8% divergence claim needs operational definition for reader verification.

annotations.text: Based on this insight, we propose search-anchored hybrid rollouts, a minimal intervention that grounds search-result observations with real data while keeping all other observations simulated. During world model rollouts, we intercept search actions and substitute the world model’s predicted search results with actual results from the WebShop search engine, cached for efficiency. This targeted grounding addresses the root cause of rollout drift without requiring improvements to the world model itself.
annotations.comment:
Paragraph role: Method proposal — introducing search-anchored hybrid rollouts.

Diagnosis: The method description is clear and concise. The core mechanism (intercept search actions, substitute with real WebShop search engine results, cache for efficiency) is well-explained. However, the paragraph does not explain why caching is valid beyond "efficiency." The BM25 determinism assumption is stated later in Section 3.3, but the introduction should briefly mention why grounding is feasible (deterministic retrieval) to establish credibility early. Also, the phrase "without requiring improvements to the world model itself" could be read as dismissive; it might be better to frame this as a complementary intervention.

Impact: Without briefly grounding the feasibility, the method may appear as an engineering workaround rather than a principled approach. The dismissive wording may alienate readers who work on world model training.

Actionable fix: Add one clause on BM25 determinism and reframe the closing sentence as a complementary perspective.

Mentor Revised Version:
Based on this insight, we propose search-anchored hybrid rollouts, a minimal intervention that grounds search-result observations with real data while keeping all other observations simulated. During world model rollouts, we intercept search actions and substitute the world model's predicted results with actual results from the WebShop search engine. Because WebShop uses a deterministic BM25 retrieval system, these results can be cached, making grounding computationally efficient. This targeted approach complements world model training by addressing the dominant error source directly.
annotations.summary: Intro P3 should briefly state BM25 determinism and reframe as complementary rather than dismissive.

annotations.text:
A CR of 1.0 indicates perfect rollout fidelity, where world model trajectories are fully executable in the real environment. Lower CR values indicate rollout drift, where simulated trajectories diverge from real environment behavior, limiting the utility of world models for planning, verification, or synthetic data generation.
3.2 MOTIVATION: SEARCH RESULTS AS THE DOMINANT ERROR SOURCE
annotations.comment:
This paragraph defines the world model formalism and the Consistency Ratio (CR) metric used throughout the paper. The formalism is clear and consistent with Word2World (Li et al., 2025), and the CR definition (W2R/Real) is correct.

Diagnosis: The paragraph is technically sound, but the notation has a minor formatting issue: the world model function signature $\mathcal{M}: \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{\bar{S}}$ appears as $\mathcal { M } : \mathcal { S } \times \mathcal { A }  \mathcal { \bar { S } }$ with a missing arrow. Additionally, the agent $\pi: \mathcal{S} \to A$ appears as $\pi : { \mathcal { S } }  A$ also missing the arrow. These are likely PDF extraction artifacts but should be verified in the source LaTeX.

More importantly, the CR metric is borrowed from Word2World without discussing its limitations. CR as W2R/Real is a ratio metric that can exceed 1.0 (as seen in Table 2 where CR = 1.034), which can be counterintuitive. The paragraph should briefly acknowledge that CR > 1.0 is possible when the world model acts as a filter.

Impact: Missing arrows reduce notation clarity. Not acknowledging CR > 1.0 can confuse readers who see values above 1.0 in results.

Actionable fix: (a) Verify LaTeX source for missing arrows in function signatures. (b) Add one sentence noting that CR can exceed 1.0 when the world model filters out unsuccessful trajectories.

Mentor Revised Version:
A CR of 1.0 indicates perfect rollout fidelity, where world model trajectories are fully executable in the real environment. Lower CR values indicate rollout drift. Note that CR can exceed 1.0 when the world model acts as a behavioral filter, excluding trajectories that would fail in the real environment.
annotations.summary: Method §3.1 needs notation verification and CR > 1.0 clarification for reader interpretability.

annotations.text:
3.3 SEARCH-ANCHORED HYBRID ROLLOUTS
We propose search-anchored hybrid rollouts, a minimal intervention that grounds search-result observations with real data while keeping all other observations simulated. Figure 1 illustrates the architecture.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph provides the motivation for the method by categorizing WebShop actions and identifying search-result simulation as the primary failure mode.

Diagnosis: The paragraph is clear and directly motivated by the diagnostic finding in the introduction. However, it defers the quantitative evidence to Section 4.3 without providing even a brief inline statistic. The phrase "Preliminary analysis reveals" is vague—readers cannot tell if this is a small-scale exploratory analysis or the full error analysis that appears in Section 4.3. The paragraph should briefly anchor the claim with the key numbers (100% first divergence at search, 99.8% per-step rate) to make the motivation self-contained.

Impact: Without inline evidence, the motivation feels like an assertion rather than a data-driven justification. This weakens the logical bridge to the method proposal in §3.3.

Actionable fix: Add one sentence with the key divergence statistics and clarify that this analysis is reported in full in Section 4.3.

Mentor Revised Version:
To understand the root cause of rollout drift, we analyze where world model predictions first diverge from real environment observations. In WebShop, agent actions can be categorized into three types: (1) search[query] actions that return ranked product lists, (2) click[ASIN] actions that navigate to product detail pages, and (3) navigation actions for page traversal and option selection. Our analysis reveals that search-result simulation is the dominant failure mode: the world model generates hallucinated product ASINs and descriptions that differ from real WebShop search results, causing cascading errors as the agent interacts with non-existent products. This finding (detailed in Section 4.3, with 100% of first divergences occurring at search observations) motivates a targeted intervention: rather than improving the world model's general prediction accuracy, we address the dominant drift source by grounding only search-result observations with real data.
annotations.summary: Method §3.2 motivation needs inline statistics to anchor the search-failure-mode claim.

annotations.text:
During a simulated rollout inside the world model, we intercept the agent’s action at each step. If the action is not a search query, we forward the (history, action) pair to the world model and use its predicted next observation. If the action is search[query], we bypass the world model’s prediction and instead fetch the search results from the real WebShop environment. This substituted observation then becomes part of the rollout history for subsequent steps.
The key insight is that WebShop observations can be decomposed into (i) relatively structured, action-conditioned state updates (e.g., navigating pages, selecting options), and (ii) a high-entropy retrieval channel (the ranked product list returned by search). A supervised world model trained on trajectories may learn (i) well but fail on (ii) because retrieval outputs depend on a large product index (1.18M products) and subtle IR details that are difficult to memorize.
To ensure determinism and efficiency, we implement a search cache that maps query strings to serialized result pages. WebShop uses a deterministic BM25-based retrieval system (Lin et al., 2021), so identical queries always return identical results. This allows us to treat search results as an exogenous observation channel rather than part of the learned world dynamics, without requiring repeated real-environment queries during evaluation.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph describes the core method: search-anchored hybrid rollouts with BM25-based caching.

Diagnosis: The method intuition is clear and theoretically well-grounded (decomposing observations into structured state updates vs. high-entropy retrieval). The BM25 determinism assumption is properly cited. However, critical reproducibility details are missing: (a) the format of substituted search results is not specified (raw HTML? serialized text? accessibility tree?), (b) the cache initialization protocol is unclear (pre-built? on-demand? size?), and (c) "exogenous observation channel" is a useful conceptual term but lacks operational definition.

Impact: Without these details, the method cannot be fully reproduced, and the theoretical framing remains partially ambiguous.

Actionable fix: Add one paragraph or extended sentence specifying: (a) search result format matches the original WebShop observation format to ensure consistent input to the agent, (b) cache is pre-built before evaluation to avoid runtime latency, (c) define exogenous channel as observations whose content is determined by external retrieval rather than learned state transitions.

Mentor Revised Version:
To ensure determinism and efficiency, we implement a search cache that maps query strings to serialized result pages in the same observation format used by the WebShop environment. The cache is pre-built before evaluation to avoid runtime latency. WebShop uses a deterministic BM25-based retrieval system (Lin et al., 2021), so identical queries always return identical results. This allows us to treat search results as an exogenous observation channel—defined as observations whose content is determined by external retrieval rather than learned state transitions—separate from the learned world dynamics, without requiring repeated real-environment queries during evaluation.
annotations.summary: Method §3.3 needs reproducibility details: search result format, cache protocol, and exogenous channel definition.

annotations.text: We evaluate on WebShop (Yao et al., 2022a), a simulated e-commerce environment with 1.18M products and 12,087 task instructions. Agents interact via text actions including search[query] for product retrieval and click[item] for navigation. We use 200 test episodes with 3 random seeds to account for agent sampling variance.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph lists the six experimental conditions organized into agent-side and observation-side baselines.

Diagnosis: The experimental design is well-structured with clear grouping. However, there is a potential confounding factor not addressed: the ReAct prompt is used both as a standalone agent-side baseline and combined with all-search anchoring. This means the "All-search anchored + ReAct" condition differs from "All-search anchored (basic)" in TWO dimensions (prompting + grounding), not just one. The small delta (CR 0.819 vs. 0.824) could be attributed to the ReAct prompt, but without an "All-search anchored + ReAct" comparison against "All-search anchored (basic)" with matched prompting, the decomposition of effects is ambiguous.

Additionally, the Best-of-N baseline uses "1-step world model lookahead," but the world model itself is the source of hallucination. Using a hallucinated world model for lookahead selection may not be a fair comparison. This should be acknowledged.

Impact: The confounding between prompting and grounding reduces the interpretability of the ablation. The Best-of-N fairness issue may weaken the claim that observation grounding addresses a different failure mode.

Actionable fix: (a) Add a brief note acknowledging that the ReAct delta is small and may not be statistically significant. (b) Note the limitation that Best-of-N uses the same hallucinated world model for lookahead.

Mentor Revised Version:
We compare six conditions organized into two groups. Agent-side baselines modify the acting agent without changing observations: (1) Pure WM: unmodified Word2World evaluation with the world model generating all observations; (2) Best-of-N (N=4): inference-time scaling where the agent samples 4 candidate actions per step and selects via 1-step world model lookahead (Wang et al., 2022); (3) ReAct prompt: enhanced prompting with explicit reasoning format and search strategy guidance (Yao et al., 2022b). Note that Best-of-N uses the same world model for lookahead, so its effectiveness is bounded by world model fidelity. Observation-side methods modify the observations returned to the agent: (4) First-search anchored: only the first search observation per episode is grounded with real data; (5) All-search anchored (basic): all search observations are grounded, using the basic prompt; (6) All-search anchored + ReAct: our full method combining all-search anchoring with the ReAct prompt.
annotations.summary: Experimental setup needs confounding acknowledgement: ReAct+anchoring decomposes two effects; Best-of-N lookahead shares the same flawed WM.

annotations.text:
Table 1 presents the main experimental results. Our proposed method, all-search anchored + ReAct, achieves the highest Consistency Ratio $( \mathbf { C R } = 0 . 8 2 \bar { 4 } \doteq 0 . 0 1 8 )$ with the lowest variance across all conditions.
Several key findings emerge from these results. First, all-search anchoring improves CR from 0.594 (pure WM) to 0.824, a +38.7% relative improvement. This demonstrates that grounding search observations substantially reduces rollout drift. Second, first-search anchoring provides negligible benefit $\left( \mathrm { C R } = 0 . 5 9 8 \ \mathrm { v s . } \ 0 . 5 9 4 \right)$ , indicating that anchoring only the initial search is insufficient— compounding errors from subsequent unanchored searches negate the benefit of grounding the first search alone. Third, observation grounding outperforms agent-side improvements: all-search anchored $( \mathrm { C R } = 0 . 8 1 9 )$ exceeds Best-of-N $( \mathrm { C } \bar { \mathbf { R } } = \bar { 0 . 7 } 4 8 )$ by +0.071, showing that grounding observations addresses a different failure mode than improving action selection. Finally, search anchoring and ReAct prompting provide complementary benefits: their combination achieves $\mathrm { C R } = 0 . 8 2 4 $ with 3.4× lower variance (std = 0.018 vs. 0.062) compared to ReAct alone, indicating that observation grounding and improved agent behavior address partially overlapping but distinct sources of rollout drift.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph presents the main results analysis with four key findings.

Diagnosis: There are two issues that affect claim validity:

1. **Rendering artifact**: The CR value is written as `$(\mathbf{CR} = 0.82\bar{4} \doteq 0.018)$` where `\doteq` appears to be a formatting error for `\pm`. The intended value is CR = 0.824 ± 0.018. This must be corrected in the LaTeX source.

2. **Mixed-effect comparison**: The +38.7% relative improvement (0.594 → 0.824) compares Pure WM to All-search anchored + ReAct. This conflates TWO interventions: observation grounding AND ReAct prompting. The claim "grounding search observations substantially reduces rollout drift" is attributed to this delta, but the ReAct component also contributes. A cleaner comparison would be Pure WM (0.594) vs. All-search anchored basic (0.819), yielding +37.9% from grounding alone, with ReAct adding only +0.005 additional CR.

Impact: The rendering error reduces professionalism. The mixed-effect attribution overstates the grounding-only gain and understates the ReAct marginal contribution, potentially misleading readers about where the value lies.

Actionable fix: (a) Fix `\doteq` to `\pm` in LaTeX source. (b) Decompose the +38.7% into grounding-only and ReAct components for clearer attribution.

Mentor Revised Version:
Table 1 presents the main experimental results. Our proposed method, all-search anchored + ReAct, achieves the highest Consistency Ratio (CR = 0.824 ± 0.018) with the lowest variance across all conditions. Several key findings emerge: First, all-search anchoring alone improves CR from 0.594 (Pure WM) to 0.819 (All-search anchored basic), a +37.9% relative improvement, demonstrating that grounding search observations substantially reduces rollout drift. Second, first-search anchoring provides negligible benefit (CR = 0.598 vs. 0.594), indicating compounding errors from subsequent unanchored searches negate the initial grounding benefit. Third, observation grounding outperforms agent-side improvements: All-search anchored (CR = 0.819) exceeds Best-of-N (CR = 0.748) by +0.071. Finally, ReAct prompting adds a small but variance-reducing complement: the combination achieves CR = 0.824 with 3.4× lower variance (std = 0.018 vs. 0.062) than ReAct alone.
annotations.summary: Main results paragraph has CR rendering error and mixed-effect attribution: +38.7% conflates grounding+ReAct effects.

annotations.text: To validate the mechanism behind search anchoring, we analyze where world model predictions first diverge from real environment observations. Figure 2 shows the per-step divergence rate across action types. Search results exhibit a 99.8% divergence rate—the world model almost never produces correct search results. In contrast, product details (50.9%) and navigation observations (68.4%) show lower divergence rates. Critically, 100% of first divergences occur at search-result observations, always at step 0. This confirms that search-result simulation is the universal initial failure point, and non-search divergences are largely downstream effects: once the world model produces incorrect search results, the agent clicks on hallucinated products, causing cascading errors.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph provides the error source analysis, anchoring the 99.8% search divergence rate and the claim that 100% of first divergences occur at search results.

Diagnosis: The analysis is the strongest empirical pillar of the paper. The 99.8% divergence rate for search vs. 50.9% for product details and 68.4% for navigation is highly convincing evidence that search simulation is uniquely broken. However, one claim needs clarification: "always at step 0." Step 0 typically means the very first action in the episode. If search actions occur at step 0 by design in WebShop, this is a dataset property, not necessarily a general property of text-based world models. The reader should know whether WebShop tasks always begin with a search action, which would make "100% at step 0" somewhat tautological.

Impact: If WebShop tasks universally start with search, then "100% at step 0" is less of a strong discovery and more of a dataset artifact. This should be acknowledged to avoid overgeneralizing.

Actionable fix: Clarify whether WebShop tasks always begin with search, and reframe the "100% at step 0" claim as "100% of first divergences occur at the first search action, which is also the first step in WebShop tasks."

Mentor Revised Version:
To validate the mechanism behind search anchoring, we analyze where world model predictions first diverge from real environment observations. Figure 2 shows the per-step divergence rate across action types. Search results exhibit a 99.8% divergence rate—the world model almost never produces correct search results. In contrast, product details (50.9%) and navigation observations (68.4%) show lower divergence rates. Critically, 100% of first divergences occur at search-result observations, which correspond to step 0 in WebShop since all tasks begin with a search action. This confirms that search-result simulation is the universal initial failure point, and non-search divergences are largely downstream effects: once the world model produces incorrect search results, the agent clicks on hallucinated products, causing cascading errors.
annotations.summary: Section 4.3's "100% at step 0" is partially a WebShop dataset property; clarify to avoid overgeneralization.

annotations.comment:
This paragraph provides stratified analysis of CR by search count, confirming that multi-search episodes benefit more from anchoring.

Diagnosis: The stratified analysis is a strong piece of evidence. The +22% improvement for ≥2 searches and +0.247 absolute improvement for ≥3 searches cleanly support the compounding-error hypothesis. However, Table 2 shows an interesting anomaly: CR for "1 search" with All-search anchored is 1.034, which exceeds 1.0. While CR > 1.0 is theoretically possible (as noted in §3.1), the text does not discuss this. A value above 1.0 suggests the world model filters out some failing trajectories, which is an interesting phenomenon worth one sentence of interpretation.

Also, the sample sizes are imbalanced: only n=37 for 1 search vs. n=163 for ≥2 searches. This should be acknowledged as a limitation for the 1-search conclusion.

Impact: Without discussing CR > 1.0 and sample imbalance, the stratified analysis lacks completeness.

Actionable fix: Add one sentence noting the CR > 1.0 anomaly and its interpretation, and one note on the small n=37 sample for 1-search episodes.

Mentor Revised Version:
To understand how search anchoring benefits scale with episode complexity, we stratify CR by the number of search actions per episode (Figure 3 and Table 2). Approximately 90% of episodes involve ≥2 search actions, making multi-search anchoring relevant for most WebShop tasks. For these episodes, all-search anchoring achieves CR = 0.624 compared to 0.513 for Pure WM (+22% relative improvement). The benefit is even more pronounced for episodes with ≥3 searches, where CR reaches 0.618 versus 0.371 for Pure WM (+0.247 absolute). Notably, 1-search episodes show CR = 1.034 with all-search anchoring, suggesting the world model may filter out failing trajectories when only one search is needed; however, this conclusion is based on a small sample (n=37). These results confirm that compounding search errors drive rollout drift and that our method targets the root cause.
annotations.summary: Section 4.4 should discuss CR > 1.0 anomaly and small n=37 sample for 1-search episodes.

annotations.text:
We identified search-result simulation as the primary failure mode in LLM-based world models for web agents and proposed search-anchored hybrid rollouts to address this limitation. By grounding only search observations with real data while keeping other observations simulated, our method improves Consistency Ratio from 0.594 to 0.824 (+38.7%) on WebShop. Our analysis reveals that compounding search errors drive rollout drift, as anchoring only the first search provides negligible benefit while anchoring all searches yields substantial gains.
Limitations. Our evaluation is limited to WebShop; generalization to other web environments (WebArena, Mind2Web) requires further investigation. The approach assumes access to a search cache or real search API, which may not be available in all deployment scenarios.
Future Work. Extending search anchoring to other high-entropy action types (e.g., API calls, database queries) and investigating learned retrieval augmentation for world models are promising directions.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph provides the Conclusion, Limitations, and Future Work.

Diagnosis: The conclusion is concise and well-structured. The limitations paragraph honestly states two key constraints: (a) evaluation limited to WebShop, and (b) requires access to a search cache/API. The future work paragraph identifies two natural extensions.

However, the conclusion reuses the +38.7% figure (0.594 → 0.824) which, as noted in the Main Results annotation, conflates grounding + ReAct. The conclusion should either decompose this or use the grounding-only figure (0.594 → 0.819, +37.9%) to maintain consistency with the more careful decomposition recommended in Section 4.2.

Also, the limitations paragraph could be strengthened by adding one more limitation: the approach assumes deterministic retrieval (BM25), which may not hold in environments with personalized or dynamic search results. This is an important boundary condition for generalization.

Impact: Reusing the conflated +38.7% figure propagates the attribution error from Section 4.2. Missing the personalization/dynamic search limitation reduces the defensibility of the generalization claim.

Actionable fix: (a) Decompose the CR improvement or use grounding-only figure. (b) Add one sentence on the deterministic-retrieval assumption limitation.

Mentor Revised Version:
We identified search-result simulation as the primary failure mode in LLM-based world models for web agents and proposed search-anchored hybrid rollouts to address this limitation. By grounding only search observations with real data while keeping other observations simulated, our method improves Consistency Ratio from 0.594 to 0.819 (+37.9% from grounding alone) on WebShop. Our analysis reveals that compounding search errors drive rollout drift, as anchoring only the first search provides negligible benefit while anchoring all searches yields substantial gains.

Limitations. Our evaluation is limited to WebShop; generalization to other web environments (WebArena, Mind2Web) requires further investigation. The approach assumes access to a search cache or real search API, which may not be available in all deployment scenarios. Additionally, our method relies on the deterministic retrieval assumption (BM25), which may not hold in environments with personalized or dynamic search results.

Future Work. Extending search anchoring to other high-entropy action types (e.g., API calls, database queries) and investigating learned retrieval augmentation for world models are promising directions.
annotations.summary: Conclusion reuses conflated +38.7% figure and should add deterministic-retrieval limitation for generalization defensibility.
